claim: No automated metric (code complexity, BLEU, ROUGE, CHRF, cosine similarity, readability scores) correlates strongly with human-judged quality of LLM-generated legacy code documentation; the strongest correlation found was only 0.34.
stance_target: Zero-Hallucination & Rigid Evals pillar — automated proxy metrics (BLEU/ROUGE-style) are insufficient to certify LLM-generated documentation quality without human review
scope_conditions: MUMPS EHR corpus and IBM mainframe Assembly Language Code corpus, 4 LLMs (Claude 3.0 Sonnet, Llama 3 70B, Mixtral 8x7B, GPT-4 Turbo)
quoted_support: The highest correlation is between the cosine similarity score and usefulness—at a correlation of just 0.34... we find no automated metrics strongly correlate with comment quality to predict or measure LLM performance.

claim: LLM-generated line-wise documentation for a MUMPS EHR legacy codebase scored above 8/10 on readability and hallucination-freedom, but on assembly language code (ALC) only readability scored above 7/10 for two of four models, with other quality dimensions falling short.
stance_target: Reverse Engineering & Codebase Mastery pillar — LLM code-understanding quality is not uniform across legacy languages; lower-level/more esoteric languages (assembly) degrade LLM documentation quality more than higher-level legacy languages (MUMPS)
scope_conditions: WorldVistA MUMPS corpus (5,107 LOC, 78 files) vs Walmart zFAM ALC corpus (13,344 LOC, 12 files); human SME evaluation, 4-point rubric
quoted_support: the LLMs perform well overall (that is, achieving greater than 8 out of 10) on creating readable and hallucination-free documentation for MUMPS... On our ALC dataset the picture is different: only on readability do we see any LLM-generated comments rated above 7/10 (Llama3 and GPT-4 Turbo at 7.28 and 7.65, respectively).

claim: Replacing ground-truth comments with unique randomly-generated placeholder IDs and requesting structured JSON output per-ID prevents LLMs from rewriting surrounding code and reduces hallucinated identifier creation during documentation generation.
stance_target: Zero-Hallucination & Quality Control pillar — a concrete prompt-engineering pattern (placeholder IDs + structured JSON output) to constrain agent blast radius during a documentation task
scope_conditions: line-wise comment generation task across 4 LLMs
quoted_support: Using unique, randomly generated identifiers also mitigated hallucination that might occur with an LLM creating its own unique identifiers. Requesting structured output, such as JSON-formatted output, provides two benefits: reduced likelihood of the LLM improvising beyond the input and instructions, and streamlined integration with downstream processes.

claim: A naive prompting strategy of asking an LLM to comment every line of legacy code caused the model to rewrite the code itself as a side effect, especially in MUMPS where 5-6 logical statements can appear on a single line.
stance_target: Zero-Hallucination & Quality Control pillar — unconstrained agent prompts for 'safe' documentation tasks can still cause unintended code modification (blast radius escape)
scope_conditions: preliminary experimentation phase, MUMPS legacy code
quoted_support: In preliminary experimentation, we found that a naive prompting strategy of feeding code into an LLM and asking it to add comments to every line was ineffective, as the models would often alter the code to generate documentation—a task outside the scope of the prompt.

claim: A prior study found LLM-based code translation among C, C++, Go, Java, and Python passed unit tests at most 47.3% of the time and as low as 2.1% in the worst-performing model, across 1,700 open-source code examples.
stance_target: Zero-Hallucination pillar — direct LLM code translation cannot be trusted for critical modernization without rigid evals/testing, even on mainstream languages
scope_conditions: cited study by Pan et al., mainstream languages C/C++/Go/Java/Python, 1,700 code examples
quoted_support: A recent evaluation by Pan et al. on 1,700 different open-source code examples, for instance, found that LLM translation among C, C++, Go, Java, and Python could produce code that passed unit tests at most 47.3% of the time and only 2.1% in the worst-performing model.

claim: The US federal government spends almost 80% of its IT budget on operations and maintenance of legacy systems, compared to about half in the private sector, and eight of ten critical federal legacy IT systems most in need of modernization lacked documented modernization plans as of the cited GAO report.
stance_target: Context for why AI-driven legacy code modernization (reverse engineering pillar) is an economically significant problem
scope_conditions: US federal government IT, per GAO reporting cited in the paper
quoted_support: Agencies are falling short in their IT modernization initiatives, spending almost 80% of their IT budgets on operations and maintenance, compared with around half in the private sector... eight of the ten critical federal IT legacy systems that were most in need of modernization did not have documented plans for modernizing their systems or had incomplete plans.
numbers: ~80% of federal IT budget on O&M vs ~50% private sector
8 of 10 critical federal legacy systems lack documented modernization plans
